parole.significato: Forming diminutive or affectionate forms of nouns or names.
parole.testo: Variant spelling of -y, with the spelling possibly influenced by the cognate Scots -ie.

parole.significato: Hypocoristic suffix
parole.testo: Modern sense in slang [circa 1936]. According to OED, a colloquial clipping of the hypocoristic diminutive suffix -sy. parole.significato: Wrong, awry, askew, amiss, or distortedly.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots agley.

parole.significato: To guide; to direct.
parole.testo: From Scots airt.

parole.significato: An oat.
parole.testo: From Scots ait, ate, from Middle English ate, from Old English āte. More at oat.

parole.significato: Solely; only.
parole.testo: From all + Scots anerly (“singly”), from ane (“one”).

parole.significato: and all; as well
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots anaw.

parole.significato: Strange, rare, unusual.
parole.testo: From Scots antrin, present participle of anter (“to adventure, venture”).

parole.significato: A large, shallow, oval dish used for serving food.
parole.testo: From the Scots form of French assiette. Doublet of assiette.

parole.significato: A receptacle under a fire grate for collecting ashes; an ash-hole.
parole.testo: From Scots ass, asse or ash + hole.

parole.significato: Days gone by; former times.
parole.testo: From Scots auld lang syne (“old long ago”, literally “old long since”), popularized by the poem “Auld Lang Syne” (1788) by Scottish poet and lyricist Robert Burns (1759–1796) based on an older song.

parole.significato: A member of the conservative party in the Church of Scotland in the latter part of the 18th century.
parole.testo: From the Scots for Old Light.

parole.significato: cloudberry, Rubus chamaemorus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots averin.

parole.significato: To hit or strike, especially with something flat or soft.
parole.testo: Probably from Scots baff, beff, bauf, probably from West Flemish baf, baffe (“a blow, slap in the face”). Compare also Old French baffe (“slap in the face”) (Modern French baffe), of imitative origin.

parole.significato: To publicly disgrace (someone); specifically, a recreant knight.
parole.testo: The origin of the verb is uncertain; it is possibly from Scots bauchle (“to annoy; to cause harm or trouble to; to disgrace; to jilt; to treat with contempt”), from bauchle (“useless or worn-out person or thing; clumsy work, bungle; clumsy or untidy person; contemptible person; laughing stock”); fur

parole.significato: A child or baby.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots bairn, from Middle English bern, barn, from Old English bearn, from Proto-West Germanic *barn, from Proto-Germanic *barną. Doublet of barn. Compare West Frisian bern.

parole.significato: Offspring; the group of all offspring.
parole.testo: From Scots bairntime, from Middle English barntem, from Old English bearntēam. Influenced by time.

parole.significato: The quality, condition, or state of a bairn (child); childhood
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots bairnheid, equivalent to bairn + -hood.

parole.significato: Bow-legged, having knees bending outward.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots bandy.

parole.significato: To misuse, to bungle.
parole.testo: From Scots, probably related to Old French bafouer (“to hoodwink”).

parole.significato: The scrotum or ballsack.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots bawbag (“ballsack”). Doublet of ballbag.

parole.significato: A coin originally worth six pennies Scots, and later three; held equivalent to an English halfpenny.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots bawbee.

parole.significato: A smart person, a bloke.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots beezer, beeser, of unknown origin. First attested in the 1910s. The adjective is from the noun.

parole.significato: Showing the effects of much weeping; marred or swollen in the face through continued weeping.
parole.testo: From Scots begrutten, past participle of begrete (“to beweep”), equivalent be- + greet (“to weep”).

parole.significato: To befool; deceive; balk; jilt.
parole.testo: Perhaps from a nasalised variant of Scots begeck (“to deceive, disappoint”), equivalent to be- + geck.

parole.significato: Beholden; indebted.
parole.testo: From Old Scots behald, behauld, reduced variant of behalden, behaulden (“beholden, indebted”), from behald, behauld (“to look at, regard”). More at behold.

parole.significato: A Scottish or Irish mountain or high peak.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots ben, benn, from Scottish Gaelic beinn.

parole.significato: A proverbial expression used to signify the futility of making detailed plans when the ability to fully or even partial…
parole.testo: Shortened form of “the best laid plans of mice and men often go awry”, translated from Scots “The best laid schemes o' Mice an' Men, / Gang aft agley,” from To A Mouse, On Turning Her Up In Her Nest With The Plough by Robert Burns (text and reading of poem).

parole.significato: A wooden drinking-cup or other dish.
parole.testo: From Scots bicker, from Middle English biker. Doublet of beaker.

parole.significato: bristle
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots birse (“bristle, hair”).

parole.significato: Dark-complexioned; swarthy
parole.testo: From Scots blackaviced, blackavised, from black + euphonic -a- (perhaps after blackamoor) + French vis (“face”) + -ed.

parole.significato: Obvious, on show; unashamed; loudly obtrusive or offensive.
parole.testo: Coined by Edmund Spenser in 1596 in "blatant beast". Probably a variation of *blatand (Scots blaitand (“bleating”)), present participle of blate, a variation of bleat, equivalent to blate + -ant. See bleat. parole.significato: Bashful, sheepish.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots blate (“timid, sheepish”), apparently a conflation of: * Northern Middle English *blate, *blait (“pale, ghastly, terrified”), from Old English blāt (“pale, livid, ghastly”), from Proto-West Germanic *blait (“pale, discoloured”), from Proto-Germanic *blaitaz, from Proto-Indo-Europ

parole.significato: bloody.
parole.testo: From Scots bluid (“blood”).

parole.significato: A kind of supernatural being.
parole.testo: From Scots boglet.

parole.significato: To thrust or push out; butt; poke.
parole.testo: From Scots bock, attested from the 16th century.

parole.significato: A tournament in the sport of curling.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots bonspiel, from Middle Scots bonspele, possibly from Dutch bond (“league”) + spel (“game”).

parole.significato: The great skua, Stercorarius skua.
parole.testo: From Scots bonxie, from Old Norse bunki.

parole.significato: To annoy, to disturb, to irritate; to be troublesome to, to make trouble for.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots bauther, bather (“to bother”). Origin unknown. Perhaps related to Scots pother (“to make a stir or commotion, bustle”), also of unknown origin. parole.significato: A rafter or cross spar of a roof especially of a cottage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots bougar, from Middle Scots bougar, bouger, bowgar (“a cross-spar in a roof”), of obscure origin; perhaps representing Old English *bogagār (“arched beam”), from boga (“bow, arch”) + gār (“spear”), with the vocalism later being influenced by Middle Scots bow (“to bow, bend”). Howev

parole.significato: The first shoots of grass or crops.
parole.testo: From Scots braird, from Old English brerd (“edge; spike, corner”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH-.

parole.significato: Overly bold or self-assertive to the point of being insensitive, tactless or impudent; shameless.
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps from Scots brash, brasch (“a violent onset; an attack or assault”). Perhaps also related to Dutch bars (“stern; strict”), German barsch (“harsh; unfriendly”), Danish barsk (“harsh; rough; tough”), Swedish barsk (“harsh; impetuous”).

parole.significato: A human child.
parole.testo: Early Modern English (c. 1500) slang term meaning "beggar's child". Possibly from Scots bratchet (“bitch, hound”), in which case it would be a doublet of brachet. Another possibility is that it was originally a dialectal word, from northern and western England and the Midlands, for a "makeshift or r

parole.significato: Bridge.
parole.testo: From Scots brig, from Old Norse bryggja, from Proto-Germanic *brugjǭ. Doublet of bridge.

parole.significato: A type of Iron Age stone tower with hollow double-layered walls found on Orkney, Shetland, in the Hebrides and parts of…
parole.testo: From Scots broch, from Old Norse borg, from Proto-Germanic *burgz. Doublet of borough and burgh.

parole.significato: A sheepfold, especially one in which to keep ewes at milking-time.
parole.testo: From Scots bucht, of uncertain origin.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; perhaps; alternatively; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: A friend or casual acquaintance.
parole.testo: First appears c. 1788, in the writings of Charles Dibdin, of uncertain origin. Possibly from *bruddy, *bruthy, a child-talk alteration of brother. Alternatively, perhaps from British colloquial butty (“companion”), also the form of an older dialect term meaning workmate, associated with coal mining.

parole.significato: Sturdy, well-built; solid, stocky.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots buirdly, alteration of earlier buirly (“burly”), of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: To boil or seethe.
parole.testo: From Scots buller (“to boil, seethe”). Of obscure origin. Probably related to Old Norse bulla (“to boil”) and Old French bullir (“to boil”), Latin bulliō (“to boil”), all from Proto-Indo-European *bew- (“swelling”).

parole.significato: To make a lot of noise.
parole.testo: From Scots buller, bullir (“to bellow, roar”), likely of North Germanic origin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bellaną (“to roar”). Compare Danish buldre (“to rumble”), Swedish bullra (“to make a noise, roar, rumble”).

parole.significato: To load (a vessel) with coal or fuel oil for the engine.
parole.testo: The origin of the noun is uncertain; the earliest sense is sense 7.1 (“box or chest, the lid of which serves as a seat”), from Scots bunker (“bench; pew; window-seat; sand pit (especially in golf); coal receptacle; sleeping berth, bunk”), from Early Scots bunker, bunkur, bonker (“a chest or box, oft

parole.significato: A warm, often hooded infant garment, as outerwear or sleepwear, similar to a sleeper or sleepsack; especially as baby b…
parole.testo: 1922, apparently from Scots buntin (“plump, short and thick (esp. of children)”), itself an old term of endearment for children (1660s); the sense “plump” dates to the 1500s, and may be related to bunt (“belly of a sail”). Possibly related to butt (“(both noun and verb sense: buttocks; strike with h

parole.significato: A period of leisure; spare time
parole.testo: From Scots bytime, equivalent to by- + time.

parole.significato: To go carefully or slowly; to take care.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots ca canny.

parole.significato: Engaging in go-slow as part of an industrial dispute.
parole.testo: From Scots ca' canny (“to go or act cautiously”).

parole.significato: An inexpensive boot or shoe made in the 19th or early 20th century for a baby or young child.
parole.testo: Of unknown origin. Possibly from Scots cack (“soft shoe”).

parole.significato: A low-bred, presuming person; a mean, vulgar fellow, especially one that cannot be trusted with a lady.
parole.testo: Short for caddie, from Scots, from French cadet, from Occitan capdet (“chief, captain”), from Latin capitellum, diminutive of caput (“head”).

parole.significato: Synonym of cadet (“a gentleman (often a younger son from a noble family) who joined the military without a commission a…
parole.testo: The noun is borrowed from Scots caddie (“military cadet; young man; ragamuffin; person engaged to run errands; person hired to assist a golfer”), from French cadet (“army cadet; younger sibling”), from capdet (“captain; chief”) (Gascony, archaic), from Late Latin capitettum, from Latin caput (“head”

parole.significato: An old woman.
parole.testo: From Scots, from Scottish Gaelic cailleach.

parole.significato: A rounded or conical heap of stones erected by early inhabitants of the British Isles, apparently as a sepulchral monum…
parole.testo: From Scots cairn, from Scottish Gaelic càrn, from Old Irish carn, from Proto-Celtic *karnos, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂- (“horn”). Compare Welsh carn, Cornish carn. Doublet of carn and horn.

parole.significato: A spell or incantation; a trifling magic trick.
parole.testo: From Middle Scots cantrip, cantrap (“a magic charm; a trick”). parole.significato: A wooden drinking-bowl with two handles.
parole.testo: From Scots cap, an alteration of earlier cop, from Middle English cop, from Old English copp (“a cup, vessel”), from Proto-West Germanic *kopp, from Proto-Germanic *kuppaz.

parole.significato: A large, black grouse of the genus Tetrao in the bird family Phasianidae, especially the western capercaillie, Tetrao u…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots capercailzie (for the -z-, see Mackenzie and tailzie), a corruption of Scottish Gaelic capall (“horse”) + coille (“of the woods”).

parole.significato: bad-tempered, quarrelsome, snappy
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots carnaptious.

parole.significato: A man; a fellow, chap.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots chield, apparently a variant form of child retained in specific senses.

parole.significato: Vomit.
parole.testo: Unknown and debated origin. Possibly a shortening of Chunder Loo, itself a presumed rhyming slang for spew (said to be derived from the cartoon character “Chunder Loo of Akim Foo”, drawn by Norman Lindsay for a series of boot-polish advertisements in the early 1900s), but the rhyming slang usage is

parole.significato: To honk or cry like a goose.
parole.testo: From Scots claik, from Old Norse klaka.

parole.significato: Frivolous or nonsensical talk; prattle; chatter.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots claver.

parole.significato: A cover to prevent heat radiation from a boiler, cylinder, etc. of a steam engine.
parole.testo: From Scots cleding, cleiding, from earlier cleething, claithing, cleithing (“clothing”), from Middle English clething (“clothing”). See cloth, clothing.

parole.significato: To hatch (a bird); (colloquial) to give birth to (a person).
parole.testo: From Scots cleck, from Old Norse klekja.

parole.significato: A large hook.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots cleek.

parole.significato: To claw, scratch.
parole.testo: From Scots cloor, from Norwegian klore (“to scratch with the fingers, scrawl”), from Old Norse klóra (“to scrawl, scratch”), klór (“a scratching”), a frequentative verb derived from Old Norse kló (“claw”). Cognate with Icelandic klóra (“to scratch”), Faroese klóra (“to scratch, tear, claw”).

parole.significato: A piece of rag.
parole.testo: From Scots [Term?]; see cloot (“cloth”).

parole.significato: To inflict a blow on; punch.
parole.testo: From Scots clour, from Early Scots clour, clowr (“a lump or swelling caused by a blow, welt”), of uncertain origin. parole.significato: Completion of the harvest season, harvesting the last sheaf of grain.
parole.testo: From Scots clyack, which is in turn from Scottish Gaelic caileag.

parole.significato: Pholis gunnellus: The rock gunnel, a ray-finned fish found in coastal waters of the North Atlantic and Arctic oceans.
parole.testo: Of unknown origin. Possibly suffixed with Scots -lock, which forms diminutives. First attested in 1794.

parole.significato: Cold, chilling.
parole.testo: From Scots cauldrife, from Old Scots "cauldrife", a compound of "cauld" and the (Scots) suffix "-rife" (compare "auldrife", "warkrife", "spendrife" etc.), from the adjective rife.

parole.significato: A loud quarrelsome fight.
parole.testo: From Scots collie-shangie, from collie (“a breed of dog”), and shangie (“an object tied to a dog's tail”). The frustration of having a shangie attached made the highly energetic collies irritable and likely to fight.

parole.significato: The wooden centering on which a bridge is built.
parole.testo: From Scots coom, of unknown origin.

parole.significato: To crouch, stoop down.
parole.testo: From Scots coor (“cower”) + -ie (frequentative).

parole.significato: Cosy.
parole.testo: From Scots, from Old Scots colsie, probably of North Germanic origin, such as Norwegian kose seg (“to have a cozy time”), from Old Norse kose sig, from koselig, koslig, perhaps ultimately from Old High German kōsa; see modern German kosen (“to cuddle”). See also English cosy.

parole.significato: Affording comfort and warmth; snug; social and comfortable.
parole.testo: From Scots cosie, from Old Scots colsie, but ultimate derivation is unknown. Possibly of North Germanic origin, such as Norwegian kose seg (“to have a cozy time”), from Old Norse kose sig, from koselig, koslig, perhaps ultimately from Old High German kōsa; see modern German kosen (“to cuddle”).

parole.significato: Grouchy, cantankerous.
parole.testo: From Scots crabbit, from crab.

parole.significato: A flatfish of the North Atlantic, witch flounder (Glyptocephalus cynoglossus).
parole.testo: From Scots craig (“a rock”). See crag.

parole.significato: A merchant's booth; a shop or tent where goods are sold; a stall
parole.testo: From Scots crame, craim, from Middle Dutch kraeme or Middle Low German krame; both from Old High German krām (“merchant tent; tent cloth”), probably ultimately borrowed from Slavic, such as Old Church Slavonic грамъ (gramŭ, “pub, inn”) or чрѣмъ (črěmŭ, “tent”). Compare West Frisian kream, Dutch kraa

parole.significato: A haddock's head stuffed with a mixture of oatmeal, suet, onions, and pepper.
parole.testo: From Scots crappit (“crammed”), from crap (“to cram”), + head.

parole.significato: To wither, wilt, shrivel.
parole.testo: From Scots crine (“to shrivel”), from Scottish Gaelic crìon (“withered”), from Old Irish crín.

parole.significato: An exclamation of astonishment or horror.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots crivvens. Attested in English from the early 20th century.

parole.significato: Any of various lichens gathered for dyeing, especially those of the genus Parmelia.
parole.testo: From Scots crottle, from Scottish Gaelic crotal.

parole.significato: To croak, make a hoarse noise.
parole.testo: From Scots croup, croop (“the croup”), from Scots croup, crowp, croop (“to croak, speak hoarsely, murmur, complain”), from Old Scots crowp, crope, croap (“to call loudly, croak”), alteration of rowp, roup, roip, rope (“to cry, cry hoarsely, roop”), from Middle English roupen, ropen, from Old English

parole.significato: A kind of weir or dam for trapping salmon.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots cruive, from Middle Scots cruve, crove, from Old Irish cró, from Proto-Celtic *kruwos, *kruwyos, from Proto-Indo-European *krewH-.

parole.significato: A coalfish (Pollachius virens).
parole.testo: From Scots cuddie; compare Gaelic cudaig, cudainn, or English cuttlefish, or cod.

parole.significato: A square piece of linen formerly worn by women instead of a cap; a kerchief.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots curch, from Middle Scots curche, from Early Scots curche (English Middle English keverchef). Doublet of kerchief.

parole.significato: To murmur or rumble.
parole.testo: From Scots curmur, likely onomatopoeic, similar to murmur.

parole.significato: A low-pitched murmuring, grumbling sound.
parole.testo: From Scots curmur.

parole.significato: to stun, to stupefy
parole.testo: From Scots dammish, probably from Middle English damagen. Doublet of damage.

parole.significato: A man very concerned about his physical appearance, refined language, and leisurely hobbies, pursued with the appearanc…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots dandy (“a fop; one who is well-dressed”). Of uncertain origin. Possibly from Dandy, a diminutive of Andrew, yet the Scots word is used also in reference to women. parole.significato: Sick; delicate.
parole.testo: From Scots donsie.

parole.significato: did not
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots didna.

parole.significato: A torn-up piece of turf, especially by a golf club in making a stroke or by a horse's hoof.
parole.testo: 1530s, Scots divot (“turf”), also spelt devat, diffat, and the earliest form (1435), duvat(e), from Scottish Gaelic dubhad, a reduced form of dubh-fhàd, literally “black sod” (compare fàl (“turf, sod”)).

parole.significato: lump
parole.testo: From Scots daud (“large piece”).

parole.significato: To stumble; to blunder.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots doit, apparently a Scots cognate of dote.

parole.significato: dovecote
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots.

parole.significato: Stern, harsh and forbidding.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots dour, possibly from Latin dūrus (“hard, stern”), via Middle Irish dúr. Compare French dur, Catalan dur, Italian duro, Portuguese duro, Romanian dur, Spanish duro. Doublet of dure.

parole.significato: Dull, dreary; melancholy.
parole.testo: From Scots dowie, apparently a form of dull + -ly.

parole.significato: To drawl; to drone.
parole.testo: From Scots drant, draunt (“droning or drawling tone”), borrowed from Scottish Gaelic dranndan, draundan (“hum, buzzing, complaint, growl, snarl”), akin to Irish drantán (“hum, buzzing, growl”).

parole.significato: A boat used in dredging
parole.testo: Probably a borrowing from Scots dreg-boat, dreg-bot, equivalent to dredge + boat.

parole.significato: To bear or endure (something); to put up with, to suffer, to undergo.
parole.testo: Probably partly borrowed from Scots dree, and partly derived from its etymon Middle English dreen, dreghen, dreogen, drien, from Old English drēogan, from Proto-West Germanic *dreugan, from Proto-Germanic *dreuganą (“to act; to work, (specifically) to do military service”), from Proto-Indo-European

parole.significato: To lower oneself from a height and drop the remaining distance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots dreep.

parole.testo: The adjective is borrowed from Scots dreich (“hard to bear, dreary, tedious, wearisome; interminable, long-winded; dull, uninteresting; slow, tardy; doleful, gloomy; baffling, difficult; difficult to reach, inaccessible”), from Middle English dregh, dri, drie (“burdensome; depressing, dismal; large,

parole.significato: Drenched, soaked.
parole.testo: From Scots drookit, of uncertain origin. See drook, drouk.

parole.significato: deposit (on a purchase, etc.)
parole.testo: From Scots arles, from Middle English erles, from Old French erres (modern French arrhes), from Latin arrha.

parole.significato: quick-tempered
parole.testo: From Scots edgy.

parole.significato: Busy, industrious, diligent.
parole.testo: From Scots eident, Scottish form of ithand.

parole.significato: Either of the Gaelic languages of Ireland and Scotland.
parole.testo: From Scots Erse (“Irish”), from earlier Ersche, Ersch, a contraction of Erisch, Erische (“Irish”), from Middle English Erische, Irische, Irisch (“Irish”). Doublet of Irish. Compare also Scots Irisch.

parole.significato: Everyone.
parole.testo: From every + cunt, after Scots everycunt.

parole.significato: To tangle or entangle.
parole.testo: From Scots fankle, (compare English fangle), equivalent to fank (“coil, noose, vang”) + -le (frequentative suffix). Doublet of fangle.

parole.significato: Effect, value; vigor.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots, aphetic form of effect.

parole.significato: Lacking purpose.
parole.testo: From Scots feckless, variant of Scots fectless (“ineffectual”) (an aphetic variant of effectless), equivalent to effect + -less.

parole.significato: To twist or turn with a screw-like motion; to screw.
parole.testo: From Scots feeze, from Old Scots fize (“screw”, noun), from Dutch vijs (“screw”), from Middle Dutch vise (“screw, windlass, winch”), from Old French vis, viz (“vise, vice”), from Latin vītis (“vine”). Doublet of vice, vise, and withe.

parole.significato: cunning, shifty
parole.testo: From Scots fendie (“able to look after oneself, thrifty, active, healthy, lively”).

parole.significato: One who holds a feu.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots feuar. By surface analysis, feu + -ar.

parole.significato: The practice, during Hogmanay, of visiting friends and family, especially to be the first person to cross a home's thre…
parole.testo: From Scots tae first-fit (“to be the first to visit at the new year”, literally “to first-foot”).

parole.significato: A complete domicile occupying only part of a building, especially one for rent
parole.testo: From an alteration (due to Scots flatt (“a level part of a structure”)) of Scots flet, flett (“inner part of a house”), from Middle English flet (“dwelling”), from Old English flet, flett (“ground floor, dwelling”), from Proto-West Germanic *flati, from Proto-Germanic *flatją (“floor”), from Proto-G

parole.significato: A dull person (especially an old man) who is behind the times, holding antiquated, over-conservative views.

parole.significato: To assemble or gather together in one place, to gather up; to congregate.
parole.testo: From Scots forgather, foregather (“to gather up, assemble”), equivalent to for- + gather. Cognate with Dutch vergaderen (“to assemble”), German vergattern (“to assemble; to assign duty”).

parole.significato: Drunk.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots fou. Compare full, a doublet.

parole.significato: A fielding practice drill where a person hits fly balls intended to be caught.
parole.testo: Uncertain; perhaps from Scots fung (“to fling, throw”).

parole.significato: A licensed beggar.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots gaberlunzie, of unknown origin.

parole.significato: A nasty person.
parole.testo: From Scots gaet.

parole.significato: Senseless; silly, foolish.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots glaikit.

parole.significato: magic
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots glamourie (“magic”), alteration of Middle English gramarie (as glamour is of Middle English gramere), from Old French grammaire, Doublet of glamour, gramarye, grammar, and grimoire.

parole.significato: A compressable cylindrical case and its contents around a shaft where it passes through a barrier, intended to prevent…
parole.testo: Early 19th century, probably from Scots glam (“vice, clamp”), probably from a variant of clam (“clam; clamp, vise”). Related to clamp.

parole.significato: Mud, slime, mire.
parole.testo: From Scots glaur, from Middle Scots glar, of unknown origin.

parole.significato: To squint; to look obliquely; to overlook things.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots.

parole.significato: To glance (at); to look sideways.
parole.testo: Of uncertain origin. Probably from Middle English glimme (“radiance, brightness”) (whence glim), Scots glim (“glance, glimpse”) or Norwegian Nynorsk glim (“glimpse, glimmer”), all from Proto-Germanic *glīmô. Compare glim, gleam, glimmer, glimpse. The noun is derived from the verb.

parole.significato: A short flash of light, usually when reflected off a shiny surface.
parole.testo: 15th century. Borrowed from Scots glint, from Middle English glenten (“to shine, gleam; flash”), probably from Old Norse *glenta, from Proto-Germanic *glantijaną, causitive of Proto-Germanic *glintaną (“to gleam, shine”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰley- (“to shine”). parole.significato: A sulky look.
parole.testo: From Scots. Compare gloat.

parole.significato: To look sullen or glum; to frown
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots glunch, of uncertain origin, possibly an alteration of glum or glump.

parole.significato: A gift for a grandchild
parole.testo: From Scots.

parole.significato: A common daisy (Bellis perennis).
parole.testo: From Scots, from Scottish Gaelic [Term?].

parole.significato: To stare or look fixedly at someone; esp. of a child or dog in anticipation of receiving food.
parole.testo: Unknown. Adapted into English from the Scots groak, growk with an unchanged meaning; groak in Scotland and growk in Ulster. The earliest recorded English usage of this term is as grouk in 1808 (see sense 2).

parole.significato: Excellent.
parole.testo: Uncertain; possibly from British dialectal groosh (“excellent, very good”) (Lothian (Scotland)), grosh (northeast Lancashire) and groshy (“having thriving vegetation; juicy and tender; of weather: good for vegetation, rainy”) (Lancashire, Yorkshire), grushie (“having thriving vegetation”) (Scotland)

parole.significato: To catch (fish) with the hands, especially by groping at the bank of a stream or under stones.
parole.testo: From Scots guddle, imitative of the splashing of water, and modelled after words like muddle and puddle, perhaps influenced by Scots gutter (“to spatter with mud”).

parole.significato: A boisterous laugh.
parole.testo: First attested in the early 18th century, originally Scots, probably onomatopoeic.

parole.significato: A large knife.
parole.testo: From Scots gully, of unknown origin.

parole.significato: To grope, especially after fish.
parole.testo: From Scots [Term?].

parole.significato: Common sense, initiative, resourcefulness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots gumption (“common sense, shrewdness; drive, initiative”); further etymology unknown, possibly connected with Middle English gome (“attention, heed”), from Old Norse gaumr (“attention, heed”), from Proto-Germanic *gaumō. English cognates include gaum (“to comprehend, understand”)

parole.significato: To remove the guts or entrails from (a person or an animal); to disembowel, to eviscerate, to gut.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots guttle, from gut (“to eviscerate”) + -le (frequentative suffix).

parole.significato: fool; clumsy, awkward person
parole.testo: From Scots gype (“foolish, awkward person”). Compare Old Norse geip (“nonsense”).

parole.significato: A low-lying meadow by the side of a river.
parole.testo: From Northern English dialectal and Scots haugh, from Northern Middle English *halgh, from Old English healh (“corner, nook”), from Proto-West Germanic *halh. Doublet of hale.

parole.significato: To hem and haw.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots haiver.

parole.significato: Wholesome; healthful.
parole.testo: Anglicised variant of Scots hailsome, equivalent to heal + -some.

parole.significato: A piece of pastureland which farm animals (chiefly cattle or sheep) have become accustomed to.
parole.testo: The noun is borrowed from Scots heft, haft (“pasture which sheep are familiar with; attachment of sheep to a pasture; number of sheep grazing on such a pasture; (obsolete) place of residence; situation”), probably from Old Norse hefð (“occupation; possession; prescriptive right”), from hafa (“to hav

parole.significato: To cause (milk) to be held in a cow's udder until the latter becomes hard and swollen, either by not milking the cow or…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots heft, from Old Norse hepta (“to bind; to hinder, impede; to hold back, restrain”), from Proto-Germanic *haftijaną (“to bind; to secure”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to hold, seize”).

parole.significato: A shed or hovel for cattle.
parole.testo: From Scots hemmel, hammel, dialectal English hemble (“hovel, stable, shed”), perhaps allied to Dutch hemel (“heaven, canopy”), German Himmel. Compare English heaven.

parole.significato: A hiding-place; a sheltered spot.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots hiddle, from Middle Scots hiddill, from Early Scots hyddyll, an alteration, due to final s mistaken for the plural ending, of hyddlys (“hiding-place, concealment”), from Old English hȳdels (“a place of concealment, hiding-place, cavern, cave”), equivalent to hide + -le. For loss

parole.significato: Acting suspiciously; strange, unusual; acting in a manner as if having something to hide, or seemingly crooked.
parole.testo: Possibly from obsolete Scots hink, from Old Norse hinka (“to limp or hobble”), probably not from Old English inca (“doubt; suspicion”). Possibly from hank (“a loop or coil or anything that curbs or restrains”). Possibly from African-American usage: hincty or hinkty.

parole.significato: An awkward adolescent youth.
parole.testo: From Scots. Compare dialectal English hobbledygee (“(with a) limping movement”); also French hobereau (“country squire”), English hobby, and Old French hoi (“today”); the original sense may have been "an upstart of today".

parole.significato: To bob up and down on horseback, as an inexperienced rider may do; to jog.

parole.significato: New Year's Eve.
parole.testo: From Scots Hogmanay, probably from Old French aguillanneuf (“last day of the year”).

parole.significato: a drink made from boiling beer to which is added nutmeg, eggs, sugar and whiskey; drunk during first footing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots het pint.

parole.significato: A frequent meeting place; a haunt; often specifically, a drinking-house or tavern.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots howf (noun, verb).

parole.significato: To draw in the parts of the body, especially with pain or cold.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots hurkle.

parole.significato: To lounge in bed for an excessive period of time; to bed rot.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots hurkle-durkle (“to lounge in bed”), from hurkle. The term was introduced into English after lexicographer Susie Dent began spreading awareness of the term in 2015, and went viral on TikTok in 2024.

parole.significato: insane or mad.
parole.testo: From archaic Scots [Term?].

parole.significato: A small island; an islet.
parole.testo: From Scots inch, from Scottish Gaelic innis.

parole.significato: elsewhere
parole.testo: From Scots ithergates.

parole.significato: To suspect.
parole.testo: From Scots jalouse, from Old French jalouser. The sense "to be jealous of" came about as a misunderstanding by southern writers, from the similarity to jealousy.

parole.significato: Trickery or misrepresentation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots joukery-pawkery (“trickery; deceit”) Attested in English since the nineteenth century. The earliest known use was in the Berkshire Chronicle in 1845.

parole.significato: Darling, sweetheart.
parole.testo: From Scots jo (“joy”), from Middle English joye, from Old French joie, from Late Latin gaudia, neuter plural (mistaken as feminine singular) of Latin gaudium (“joy”), from gaudēre (“to be glad, rejoice”). Doublet of joy and gaudy (“Oxford college reunion”).

parole.significato: To evade, to dodge, to duck; also, to swerve.
parole.testo: From Scots jouk.

parole.significato: the part of a rotating shaft or axle that rests on the bearing
parole.testo: Unknown, apparently of Scots origin. Perhaps from chirnel, from English kernel (“lump in the flesh”), owing to resemblance in shape.

parole.significato: To deceive or outmaneuver someone using a feint, especially in American football or soccer.
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps from Scots jouk, jowk, juke (“to elude, cheat; duck, skulk; bob, dodge”), palatalized variants of Scots deuk, douk, dowk (“to duck”). More at duck (verb).

parole.significato: A round hill or short ridge of sand or gravel deposited by a melting glacier.
parole.testo: From Scots, from Middle English cambe (“comb”).

parole.significato: A traditional Fair Isle fisherman's cap.
parole.testo: From Scots kep, variant of cap.

parole.significato: A disorderly outburst, disturbance, commotion, or tumult.
parole.testo: Probably from Scots curfuffle, equivalent to ker- + fuffle, or related to Irish cíor thuathail (“confusion, bewilderment”). Similar to modern Welsh cythrwfl (“uproar, trouble, agitation”)

parole.significato: Having attended church for the first time after a wedding, birth, or other significant event.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots kirkit.

parole.significato: Either of two small gulls in the genus Rissa of the family Laridae that nest in colonies on sea cliffs and spend the wi…
parole.testo: Originally Scots, imitative of the bird's call.

parole.significato: A toilet.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots [Term?].

parole.significato: A small wooden drinking vessel with an upright handle
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots [Term?].

parole.significato: common daisy (Bellis perennis)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots cockaloorie, from Norn kokkeluri.

parole.significato: A thermal insulation sleeve for cans or bottles.

parole.significato: The hook that develops in the lower jaw of an adult male of most salmonid species when it is ready to spawn.
parole.testo: From Scots kip, kipp (“something beaked or hooked”); perhaps related to Middle Low German kippe (“point, tip”), German Kippe (“stub”), both from Latin cippus (“stake, post, boundary marker”).

parole.significato: A feudal lord in Scottish contexts.
parole.testo: The noun is borrowed from Scots laird, from northern or Scottish Middle English lard, laverd, a variant of lord. The verb is derived from the noun. Doublet of hlaford and lord.

parole.significato: A beating; a thrashing; a drubbing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots laldy, laldie.

parole.significato: Used to wish someone well, especially as a drinking toast or a farewell.

parole.significato: A golf course, especially one situated on dunes by the sea.
parole.testo: From Scots links (“sandy, rolling ground near seashore”), linkis, from Old English hlincas (“rising grounds, hills”).

parole.significato: A tall person.
parole.testo: The term originated in the United States, and was presumably used in vaudeville performances. It was derived from earlier Scots lang drink.

parole.significato: Expressing surprise, wonder etc.
parole.testo: From Scots losh.

parole.significato: To beat; to deal a heavy blow; to whack
parole.testo: From Scots.

parole.significato: A chimney; also, the top part of a chimney.

parole.significato: A poet writing in Scots.
parole.testo: From Scots makar. Doublet of maker.

parole.significato: Dismal; gloomy; grim; forbidding.
parole.testo: From Scots malagrugrous.

parole.significato: To cause havoc to; to disarrange, put into disarray.
parole.testo: From Scots malagruize.

parole.significato: destitute of grace, propriety, or moderation; uncivil; immoderate
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots menseless, equivalent to mense + -less.

parole.significato: An unattractive or ugly person.
parole.testo: See minging (from Scots mingin) and -er.

parole.significato: Very unattractive; ugly.
parole.testo: From Scots mingin (“stinking”), present participle of ming (“to stink”), from Middle English mengen (“to mix”), from Old English mengan (“to mix”).

parole.significato: Late twilight, dusk; darkening of evening.
parole.testo: From Scots mirken (“to grow dark, darken, become overcast”), from Old Norse myrkna (“dark, gloomy”) + -ing (noun-forming suffix), equivalent to mirken + -ing.

parole.significato: Dizziness; lightheadedness.
parole.testo: From Scots mirligoes (“dizziness”).

parole.significato: the northern lights
parole.testo: * Said to be from Scots mirrie (“merry”) + dancers. * That may be a false cognate. See discussion at shetnews.co.uk Community/History in a wird, 1 March 2023. Mirr can mean 'to shimmer', among other senses.

parole.significato: A domestic cat, especially (depreciative or derogatory) a non-pedigree or unremarkable cat.
parole.testo: Unknown, but probably originally Mog + -y, a Scots or Northern English variant of maggie (“girl”), from Maggie, a diminutive of Margaret and Margery. First attested in reference to mongrel cats in Cockney.

parole.significato: A large cup for beverages, usually having a handle and used without a saucer.
parole.testo: Early 16th century (originally Scots and northern English, denoting "earthenware, pot, jug"), of unknown origin, perhaps from North Germanic (compare Swedish mugg (“mug, jug”), Norwegian mugge (“pitcher, open can for warm drinks”), Danish mugge), or Low German mokke, mukke (“mug”), German Low German

parole.significato: A mischievous person; a scallywag.
parole.testo: From Scots nickum, a suffixed form of Nick.

parole.significato: tight-fitting
parole.testo: From Scots nip (“to pinch”).

parole.significato: An aquatic horse-like demon from Orcadian mythology, said to cause droughts and epidemics and to harm crops and animals.
parole.testo: From Orcadian Scots knoggelvi, from Scots neugle (“water spirit in the form of a horse”). Related to English nicker (“water demon”).

parole.significato: An idiot, dolt or fool.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots numpty (“fool, idiot”).

parole.significato: Fluff, particularly from a textile source such as cotton or wool.
parole.testo: From Scots oose, an alternative form of oos, the plural form of oo (“wool”).

parole.significato: parrot (bird)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots papingo, ultimately from Old French papegai. Cognate to popinjay, German Papagei, Dutch papegaai.

parole.significato: A Scottish crab soup made with cream and rice.
parole.testo: Scots; partan is Gaelic and Scots for crab, and bree (cognate to brew) is Scots for soup.

parole.significato: To pant, to struggle for breath.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots pech, apparently of imitative origin.

parole.significato: Small, little.
parole.testo: Scots peedie, alteration of peerie. Compare Swedish pytte.

parole.significato: Pale, pasty; off-color or ill-looking.
parole.testo: From Scots peely-wally.

parole.significato: spinning top
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots peerie.

parole.significato: A porpoise.
parole.testo: From Scots pellock, of unknown origin.

parole.significato: To fill up, to stock or supply (something).
parole.testo: Scots plenish, from pleniss- the stem of Anglo-Norman plenir in certain conjugated form, from plein (“full”). Compare replenish.

parole.significato: The police.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots polis. Doublet of police, policy, and polity.

parole.significato: Either of two lean, white marine food fishes, of the genus Pollachius, in the cod family.
parole.testo: From Middle English [Term?], perhaps from Scots podlok.

parole.testo: Origin unknown. Perhaps from Scots pud (“little fat man”, a term of endearment) (see podge) or from pudendum.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots putt (“to put”). Compare Middle Dutch putten (“to dig a pit”). parole.significato: Affectedly nice, prim.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots queem. Compare English queem.

parole.testo: From Scots rampage, equivalent to ramp + -age. Perhaps influenced by Middle English rampnen (“to force, ram”), from Old English *hrampian, from Proto-West Germanic *hrampōn (“to obstruct, hinder”), see ramp.

parole.testo: From Scots relevant meaning "legally pertinent," used in Scottish legal circles starting in the early 1500s, and first used in English in the 1700s. parole.significato: A loose, disordered collection of things; a heap; a jumble.
parole.testo: From Scots rickle, from Old English hrēac (“stack”) with the Scots suffix -le (“full (of)”).

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of Rutherglen in Scotland.
parole.testo: From Scots Ruglen (the Scots term for Rutherglen, likely also derived from Scottish Gaelic An Ruadh-Ghleann (“the red valley”)) + -ian.

parole.significato: clothed
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots sarkit, past participle of sark (“to clothe in or provide with a shirt”).

parole.significato: A fool, an idiot.

parole.significato: A poor golf shot, where the club hits the ground before it hits the ball.

parole.significato: To scrape the feet while walking.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots scunner, skunner, from Old Scots skunnyr, skowner (“to shrink back; flinch”), from Middle English skoneren (“to feel sick or disgusted”), of uncertain origin. parole.significato: An armhole (or, occasionally, a leghole) in tailoring and dressmaking.

parole.significato: A benevolent or beneficially-inclined fairy.
parole.testo: From Scots sely, seelie (“holy, good”), from Middle English seely, from Old English sǣliġ, gesǣlig. Doublet of silly.

parole.significato: Grain fallen to the ground and left after harvest.
parole.testo: Obsolete variant of shake. Compare Scots shag (“refuse of barley or oats”).

parole.significato: An area of summer pasture used for cattle, sheep etc.

parole.significato: Skilful.
parole.testo: From Scots skeely, Scottish form of skilly.

parole.significato: A fisherman's hut in Orkney.

parole.significato: A small rocky island which may be covered by the sea at high tide or during storms.

parole.significato: To make a shrill sound, as of bagpipes.
parole.testo: Originally from Scots and Northern English dialects (as a verb), probably of Old Norse origin; ultimately imitative.

parole.significato: A devious device or trick.

parole.significato: A dirty or slovenly person.
parole.testo: Possibly borrowed from Scots slait, slate (“dirty, slovenly, or objectionable person”), further etymology unknown.

parole.significato: Specious, flattering; cunning.
parole.testo: From Scots sleekit, Scottish form of sleeked. Compare slick, sleek.

parole.significato: A stew of meat and vegetables.
parole.testo: Uncertain, but said to derive from slime and Scots gullion (“swamp; cesspool”). Attested from the late nineteenth century in reference to a watery beverage (see quotation below). Compare Irish góilín (“a creek; a small inlet”).

parole.significato: An elitist or snobbish person.
parole.testo: From Scots snoot, snout (“snout”), from Middle English snowte, from Middle Dutch snute; ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *snūt, from Proto-Germanic *snūtaz. Doublet of snout.

parole.significato: lucky; fortunate; thriving; plump
parole.testo: From Scots, from Scottish Gaelic sonasach.

parole.significato: A sparrow.

parole.significato: To divine; foretell.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots spae.

parole.significato: prophet; diviner
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots spaeman.

parole.significato: female fortuneteller
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots spaewife.

parole.significato: A split dried haddock or other small fish.
parole.testo: From Scots speld (“to spread out”); compare German spalten (“to split”).

parole.significato: A curling tournament.
parole.testo: From the Scots spiel (“game, play; curling match”) from Middle Dutch or Middle Low German spel.

parole.significato: Firmly or solidly built.

parole.significato: To stitch (sew with a needle).

parole.significato: The disruption caused by a disagreement or misunderstanding.
parole.testo: Probably from Scots stooshie, possibly a contraction of English ecstasy. Perhaps related to English stoush.

parole.significato: To stretch; make straight.
parole.testo: From Scots straucht (“stretched, stretched out”). Compare Scots strauchten (“to straighten”).

parole.significato: A penis.

parole.significato: topless in warm weather.
parole.testo: From Scots taps (“tops”) aff (“off”).

parole.significato: A tithe.

parole.significato: To perfection; fully, wholly.
parole.testo: From Scots, perhaps a rebracketing of to then eyne (“to the eyes”) or to thyn eyne (“(up) to your eyes”).

parole.significato: A dowry.
parole.testo: From Scots tocher, from Middle Irish tochar.

parole.significato: To barter or trade, especially outside a government monopoly.
parole.testo: From Scots troak.

parole.significato: A stupid or foolish person, idiot.

parole.significato: Strange, weird.

parole.significato: A malevolent or malicious fairy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots unseely (“mischievous, evil-doing”), from Middle English unsely, from Old English unsǣliġ. Doublet of unsilly.

parole.significato: Exhausted; tired.
parole.testo: Scots wabbit, ultimate origin uncertain.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Scots wincey, a clipping of linsey winsey, from Middle Scots linsiewinsie, assimilated variant of linsiwolsie (“linsey-woolsey”).

parole.testo: Attested since the 16th century; borrowed from Scots wow; ultimately a natural exclamation.

parole.significato: You (plural).

parole.significato: To pull (something) with a quick, strong action.
parole.testo: Attested since 1822; from Scots yank. Unknown origin.

parole.testo: Either borrowed from Scots halesome (from Middle Scots halsum, thence Northern Middle English halesum), or formed anew from hale + -some.
